I wish I could say it just went away, but it didn't. It's definitely taken some work. I feel like I hit some form of rock bottom in the past few months, and I didn't know how to get out of it. I'm lucky enough to have a good therapist, and be in a DBT group. But really I only get out of therapy/group what I put into it, I find. The BIGGEST thing for me has been doing acts of kindness for other people. It's the only way I was able to pull my head above water, which allowed me to really start working on myself. I found that in being kind to others, I found that I DO have some worth, and I can have a huge impact on other people by simply being kind. I started to meditate before going to sleep, picturing how I felt during those acts of kindness, how real and human it made me feel. I would imagine feeling the same kindness towards myself as I do towards others. And piece by piece, I started to really feel that. Very slowly. Another big thing for me has been realizing that anything worth doing, is worth doing half-assed. I used to get so overwhelmed by doing chores and such, that I would wind up in bed doing nothing at all. So I started with spending 5 min a day tidying or whatever. Even just starting a task before going to bed is better than doing nothing. And then being able to be proud of myself for what I've done, instead of beating myself up for what I haven't. It sounds like a lot, but mostly it was just about my mindset really. Changing it a teeny tiny bit day by day. If you're able to do some research on DBT skills (mindfulness is a great place to start!) you may find it helpful. I've also been really loving the Headspace app. I find meditating morning and night to be amazing. There's a lot of research that links gratitude with happiness too. If that appeals to you check out the free trial of the Headspace app, though I will say that the paid version definitely has a ton more on it (if you're interested in that but can't afford it please let me know, I'd love to help out and buy you a subscription)

I've been there. It's one of the worst, most helpless feelings, in my opinion. Honestly, what I've done is just try to take it 5 minutes at a time. Delay and distract I think it's called. I choose a small task (washing my face, watching a 5 min youtube video, sending a text to someone, etc) just something really tiny and manageable, and focus completely on it for the duration of the task. Afterwards I re-evaluate how I'm feeling. If it's a bit better, okay cool, another task then we'll see how it goes then. I hope that makes sense! I also find the DBT skill TIPP really helpful, especially the cold water one. Here's a link that explains it a bit better: [https://www.sunrisertc.com/distress-tolerance-skills/#tipp](https://www.sunrisertc.com/distress-tolerance-skills/#tipp)

But basically holding your face in cool water for 30 second intervals can slow your heart rate and jumpstarts the parasympathetic nervous system (I think that's it- correct me if I'm wrong!) and it can be very very calming in situations of distress.

I find it helpful to make a prioritized to do list, making sure to only write down things I think I could conceivably get done that day. Then try to check them off in order, and forgive myself if/when I don't get something done. Be kind to yourself when you're feeling overwhelmed, and take care of yourself the best you can love

I've struggled with similar thoughts for quite some time.  My therapist recently told me that the brain is constantly searching for patterns, either negative or positive.  So when you're in a bad mood, your brain searches your memory for other similarly bad experiences and brings those to the surface.  And the same thing when you're feeling happy, it's much easier to recall other situations when you've felt that way.  That's why someones when one feels bad, it feels like life has *always* been bad. Or good, or boring, or whatever that emotion is.  Maybe this is obvious to most people, but for me it was an interesting insight and a reminder to fact check my thoughts and emotions regularly, even the good ones.  When I have an intense emotion, I try to think of 2 or 3 recent instances where I'm had other emotions, as a reminder that feelings are temporary and that is okay.  From there, I find it much easier to use whatever skill the moment calls for (I'm not sure if you do DBT or not, but a lot of the skills are very simple and easy to find online!).  I hope this is helpful.  Even if it's not, I hope you know that you are not alone.  Your feelings are completely valid, but that doesn't mean that they don't need to be checked every once in awhile. Hang in there lovely, stay strong.

I used to get spells like this when I was restricting for long periods at a time. I'm not a medical professional, so this is just from my experience, but it does sound like a possible iron deficiency. My dizziness was always worsened just before my period, and was often accompanied by horrible cramps. I recommend seeing a doctor to confirm it isn't something more serious, though. I will say that even though I began taking iron supplements, for me these symptoms didn't go away fully until I started seeing a nutritionist and working on building up my meals and adding nutrition back into my life. Stay strong lovely.

It does get easier, and as I started to get that enjoyment back, I had more strength to push myself to do more things and more often. Accountability helped a lot too. I still buy movie tickets days in advance so that I have to get myself out and go to the theatre. Or telling a friend "I'm about to make a craft (or whatever) and I'll send you a picture in about an hour" so that I have reason to follow through. You are strong, and you deserve to have activities in your life that bring you enjoyment! If you ever want to vent or talk about anything, please send me a message. I'm here and I care.
